paragraphs: Ranking objects usually requires many questions about which of two objects comes first. This paper asks when relationships among the objects can reduce that burden. Its central assumption is geometric: objects lie in a d-dimensional Euclidean space, and their ordering follows their distances from one shared reference point. That structure restricts which rankings are possible.

Under this assumption, the number of possible rankings grows like n raised to the power 2d. The authors develop an algorithm that chooses comparisons adaptively, using previous answers to guide subsequent questions. For a randomly selected ranking, it needs only slightly more than d log n comparisons on average. The qualification matters: this is an average result within the stated geometric setting.

The analysis also shows that randomly choosing comparisons can require almost every pair to identify a ranking. Thus, selecting informative questions is central to the savings. The paper additionally proposes an error-tolerant method for comparisons that are only probably correct, with synthetic and real-data experiments supporting the theoretical conclusions.
neurips-2011-active-ranking-using-pairwi.tldr: Under a geometric ranking assumption, adaptively chosen pairwise comparisons can identify rankings with far fewer questions on average.

paragraphs: Online decision making involves choosing actions repeatedly while learning from their losses. Hedge is a common algorithm for this setting, but its behavior depends on a learning rate. The paper identifies a drawback of tuning that rate for the hardest possible situations: the resulting method can fail to exploit easier problems, including those with one clearly superior action.

The proposed method adjusts the learning rate to the difficulty encountered during learning. Its guarantees preserve optimal worst-case performance while allowing much smaller regret on easy instances. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison action, so reducing it means paying less for the process of discovering which choices work well.

A particularly strong result applies in a probabilistic setting where one action has strictly lower average loss than every alternative. Under that condition, the adaptive method achieves constant regret, rather than regret that keeps growing with the number of rounds. A simulation study compares the approach with existing methods. Together, the contributions connect conservative worst-case protection with stronger performance when the problem permits it.
neurips-2011-adaptive-hedge-5b4cc6e2b4.tldr: Adaptive Hedge adjusts its learning rate to achieve smaller regret on easy problems while preserving optimal worst-case guarantees.

paragraphs: Channel decoding can be represented as inference in a graphical model, where the task includes estimating the probabilities of individual variables. Loops in the graph complicate this calculation. The paper studies an approximation that combines expectation propagation with a tree structure, examining whether it helps on sparse graphs of the kind used in coding theory to approach channel capacity.

Tree-based approximations are typically applied to graphs containing short cycles. The contribution here is to demonstrate their usefulness when loops extend over longer ranges. Sparsity does not remove all dependencies, and a tree approximation can still capture relationships that matter for estimating individual variables in practical code graphs.

The results distinguish two regimes. For asymptotically large sparse graphs, the method produces an approximation in which all variables are disconnected. For practical graphs of finite length, however, the tree structure provides accurate marginal estimates. This distinction explains why the behavior in an infinite-size limit does not by itself describe the value of the approximation for finite channel-decoding problems.
neurips-2011-an-application-of-tree-stru.tldr: Tree-structured expectation propagation provides accurate variable marginals for practical finite sparse code graphs with long loops.

paragraphs: A neuron may respond to only a few features of a stimulus, even when the stimulus itself has many dimensions. This paper develops a model-based interpretation of methods that identify those features from neural spikes. It connects the spike-triggered average and covariance to an expected log-likelihood formulation of a Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson model under Gaussian stimulation.

That connection makes it possible to extend familiar estimators beyond their original setting. The authors define maximum-likelihood and Bayesian estimators that are statistically consistent and efficient across a wider range of conditions, including naturalistic, non-Gaussian stimuli. Bayesian inference also supplies ways to smooth estimates, encourage sparsity, compare models, and express uncertainty through confidence intervals on model parameters.

The paper further introduces an empirical Bayes method for choosing how many stimulus features to retain. It expands the response model to allow an arbitrary elliptical nonlinear function, making feature-space inference more flexible. Validation uses extracellular recordings from macaque primary visual cortex. The contribution is both an interpretation of established statistics and a framework for richer neural-response estimation.
neurips-2011-bayesian-spike-triggered-co.tldr: A probabilistic interpretation of spike-triggered statistics enables more flexible Bayesian estimation of the stimulus features that drive neural responses.

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly a linear support vector machine can be learned. Its focus is the computational cost of optimization as the training set grows. The proposed approach combines two stochastic updates within a primal-dual formulation, linking the update of the predictor to the update of weights that determine the importance assigned to training information.

On the primal side, the method resembles stochastic gradient descent with importance weighting. On the dual side, it makes a stochastic adjustment to those importance weights. These are coupled parts of the optimization procedure: the weights participate in learning rather than serving only as a fixed choice made before optimization begins.

The stated result is an optimization method whose dependence on training-set size is sublinear. The authors also claim the first linear-SVM learning method with runtime below the size of the training set required for learning. The significance is a computational one: the amount of data associated with a learning problem need not dictate a proportional amount of optimization work. The claim concerns linear SVM learning and the proposed stochastic primal-dual approach.
neurips-2011-beating-sgd-learning-svms-i.tldr: A stochastic primal-dual method learns linear SVMs with sublinear dependence on training-set size by jointly updating the predictor and importance weights.

paragraphs: Networks evolve through events occurring over time, and understanding that evolution requires models that account for changing relationships. This paper introduces a regression framework for network event data in continuous time. It draws on survival and event-history analysis, connecting the timing of events with quantities that describe the network and its development.

The framework allows both network statistics and regression coefficients to vary with time. These provide two distinct forms of flexibility: the network properties entering the model can change, and the relationship between those properties and events can also change. The authors additionally develop an efficient inference procedure intended to make estimation feasible for large networks.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the inference procedure can accurately estimate the regression coefficients. Those estimates help interpret how the network evolves, while predictions provide a separate assessment of the fitted model. The learned model has systematically better predictive performance than the standard baselines used in the experiments. The findings therefore support both interpretability and predictive usefulness within the evaluated settings.
neurips-2011-continuous-time-regression-.tldr: A continuous-time regression framework models evolving network events with changing statistics and coefficients, supporting scalable inference and improved empirical prediction.

paragraphs: Factoring a large noisy matrix can demand substantial computation. Divide-Factor-Combine, or DFC, addresses that cost by organizing the work into smaller pieces. The framework first divides a matrix-factorization task into subproblems, then solves those subproblems in parallel, and finally combines their solutions into an answer for the original task.

DFC can use an arbitrary matrix-factorization algorithm as its base solver. Its main contribution is therefore a way to organize and combine computation rather than a single replacement factorization routine. The combination stage uses techniques from randomized matrix approximation, providing a principled bridge between solutions obtained separately and the larger matrix they collectively describe.

Experiments involving collaborative filtering, video background modeling, and simulated data demonstrate speedups ranging from near-linear to super-linear. These are attainable results in the reported experiments, rather than a universal speedup guarantee. Separately, the analysis establishes high-probability recovery guarantees comparable to those of the underlying solver. Together, these findings indicate that dividing the work can yield substantial computational gains while retaining comparable theoretical recovery assurance.
neurips-2011-divide-and-conquer-matrix-f.tldr: DFC parallelizes noisy matrix factorization through smaller subproblems while retaining recovery guarantees comparable to its base solver.

paragraphs: Classification becomes computationally demanding when an image may belong to one of many thousands of classes. A label tree organizes those classes into a hierarchy, with classifiers at its nodes guiding the decision. This paper develops a way to learn such a tree efficiently while accounting for both prediction accuracy and computational cost.

The key idea is to learn the tree structure and its node classifiers together. These choices are closely related: the arrangement of classes determines which distinctions a node must make, while the classifiers determine how effectively those distinctions can be resolved. Joint learning allows finer control over the efficiency–accuracy trade-off and leads to more balanced trees.

The authors evaluate the method on image classification involving 10,184 classes and nine million images. Relative to the previous state-of-the-art approach identified in the abstract, they report significant improvements in test accuracy and efficiency, shorter training time, and better tree balance. These results support the practical value of treating hierarchy design and classifier learning as one coordinated problem at large scale.
neurips-2011-fast-and-balanced-efficient.tldr: Jointly learning a label tree and its node classifiers improves the balance, accuracy, and efficiency of large-scale image classification.

paragraphs: Image-matching systems often compare descriptors built from local gradient statistics, such as the directions of intensity changes. Euclidean distance is a common comparison rule, with a Gaussian noise model providing a familiar probabilistic justification. This paper examines that modeling choice and finds that gradient-based descriptors often have heavy-tailed statistics, making large deviations more prominent than a Gaussian model suggests.

The authors argue that the comparison rule should follow a probability model that fits the observed descriptor distribution. They construct a similarity measure from a likelihood-ratio test and instantiate it with a Gamma-compound-Laplace distribution. The essential change is to let the statistical behavior of the descriptors shape how differences between them are judged.

For SIFT feature matching, the proposed measure produces significant improvement over existing distances at relatively low computational cost. The empirical finding concerns this matching application. More broadly, the paper challenges the probabilistic rationale for routine Euclidean comparison when descriptor statistics are heavy-tailed, and demonstrates a practical alternative grounded in the measured distribution.
neurips-2011-heavy-tailed-distances-for-.tldr: A likelihood-based distance matched to heavy-tailed descriptor statistics improves SIFT feature matching at relatively low computational cost.

paragraphs: Automatically describing an image requires connecting visual content with language. This paper approaches that problem using a large collection of photographs paired with captions. A central contribution is the collection process itself: the authors issue many Flickr queries and filter the noisy results to obtain one million images whose captions are relevant to what the pictures show.

The size and visual relevance of that collection make relatively simple non-parametric description methods effective. These methods use the available examples as a basis for describing images. The result emphasizes how the construction of a large, useful image–language collection can support a challenging task without requiring every aspect of visual description to be captured by a complicated fitted model.

The authors also develop methods that incorporate multiple estimates of image content, even though those estimates are fairly noisy. They report that this produces more pleasing descriptions. Finally, the paper introduces an objective performance measure for image captioning. Its contributions therefore span data collection, description methods, and evaluation, with the reported effectiveness tied to the demonstrated approaches.
neurips-2011-im2text-describing-images-u.tldr: A filtered collection of one million captioned photographs supports effective image descriptions using relatively simple non-parametric methods.

paragraphs: Topic models seek recurring semantic themes in text, potentially helping people search, browse, and understand document collections. Their usefulness depends on whether the resulting topics make sense to readers. Small collections and noisy text, including search snippets and blog posts, can produce themes that are difficult to interpret and consequently less useful for these applications.

The paper proposes two ways to regularize topic-model learning using external data. Both create a structured prior over words that reflects broader patterns found outside the target collection. This prior guides learning toward more coherent topics while the model still learns from the particular documents it is meant to represent.

Across thirteen datasets, both regularizers improve topic coherence and interpretability while preserving a faithful representation of the collection of interest. That combination matters because readable topics must also describe the actual documents to support useful browsing or retrieval. The findings show that external patterns can guide topic learning without replacing the collection-specific information, broadening the range of text for which topic models can be useful.
neurips-2011-improving-topic-coherence-w.tldr: Two regularizers use external word patterns to make learned topics more coherent while preserving their fit to the target collection.

paragraphs: Changes in synaptic strength are central to learning, but observing them in living brains is difficult because intracellular recordings are challenging. This paper develops two methods for estimating changes in coupling between pairs of neurons from extracellular spike recordings. The goal is to use the timing of observable neural activity to infer how the relationship between neurons changes.

The first method uses a generalized bilinear model with Poisson output and assumes that all coupling changes depend on spike timing. Under that assumption, it estimates the modification function describing spike-timing-dependent plasticity from paired spike trains. The second method uses recursive point-process adaptive filtering to estimate a broader range of time-varying coupling, relaxing the restriction to exclusively timing-dependent changes.

In simulations of neurons undergoing spike-timing-dependent modification, the authors show recovery of the true modification function. They then illustrate the technique using multi-electrode recordings from motor cortex. These two forms of evidence serve different purposes: simulations support recovery against a known process, while the recordings demonstrate application to in vivo data.
neurips-2011-inferring-spike-timing-depe.tldr: Two methods infer changing neural coupling from spike trains, including timing-dependent plasticity under an explicit modeling assumption.

paragraphs: Vector autoregressive models describe time-series relationships, but reliable sequences can be difficult to collect. A process may evolve slowly, or repeated measurements of the same process may be inaccessible. This paper considers situations where a small amount of sequence data is available alongside many easier-to-collect snapshots that lack temporal ordering.

The proposed methods incorporate those snapshots into penalized least-squares estimation of a vector autoregressive model. The essential assumption is that the non-sequence observations come from the model's stationary distribution. This gives the snapshots a specific statistical connection to the dynamics, allowing them to contribute information even though they do not reveal which observation followed which.

The authors use the discrete-time Lyapunov equation to construct a penalty based on the covariance of that stationary distribution. This connects the model estimated from sequences with distributional information supplied by snapshots. Experiments on synthetic and video data demonstrate the effectiveness of the methods. The contribution is a way to combine limited temporal evidence with abundant unordered observations under the stated stationary-distribution assumption.
neurips-2011-learning-auto-regressive-mo.tldr: Unordered snapshots help estimate vector autoregressive models when they are treated as samples from the dynamics' stationary distribution.

paragraphs: An image can contain several semantic concepts, making categorization a multi-label problem. This paper treats the assignment of labels to test images as a matrix-completion task. It constructs a data matrix containing features from both training and test images together with known training labels; the unknown test labels become entries to be filled in.

The authors propose two convex completion algorithms built around a rank-minimization criterion tailored to visual data, and establish convergence properties. The formulation connects visual features and labels within the same completion problem. This makes their shared structure central to prediction, rather than treating the unknown labels as a separate output disconnected from the matrix representation.

The paper identifies robustness to outliers, background noise, and partial occlusions in feature and label space as a major advantage over standard discriminative approaches. Experiments on several datasets show better performance than the state-of-the-art algorithms evaluated, while capturing semantic class concepts. The results support matrix completion as a practical formulation for multi-label image categorization in those tested settings.
neurips-2011-matrix-completion-for-multi.tldr: Multi-label image classification is formulated as matrix completion, using convex algorithms that exploit shared feature–label structure and robustness to corruption.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems allow multiple correct outputs, each of which has an internal structure. Examples include object detection, biological secondary structures, and graph matching with symmetries. Conventional multi-label methods typically require listing the label space explicitly, which becomes infeasible when the possible outputs are complex structured objects.

Simply applying methods designed for single-label structured prediction creates another difficulty. According to the paper, doing so can reduce accuracy or produce optimization problems that cannot feasibly be solved. The authors derive a maximum-margin training formulation specifically for the multi-label structured setting, aiming to retain high prediction accuracy without making training computationally intractable.

The resulting formulation preserves several useful properties of single-label maximum-margin learning. Training is expressed as a convex optimization problem, supports efficient working-set methods, and comes with PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds. These contributions address different aspects of the same challenge: representing multiple structured answers, making the optimization manageable, and providing theoretical support for performance beyond the training examples.
neurips-2011-maximum-margin-multi-label-.tldr: A maximum-margin formulation makes multi-label structured prediction computationally tractable while preserving convex training and generalization guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper introduces fragmentation-coagulation processes as Bayesian nonparametric models for collections of sequences. Their changing state is a partition: a grouping of sequences into clusters. As the process moves along the sequence, clusters can split or merge, allowing the grouping to evolve without committing to a fixed number of clusters.

The construction is exchangeable, projective, stationary, and reversible, with equilibrium distributions supplied by the Chinese restaurant process. Compared with hidden Markov models, the authors emphasize flexible cluster counts and avoidance of label-switching non-identifiability. Representing groupings directly makes the partition central, avoiding ambiguity caused by assigning different names to otherwise equivalent clusters.

To fit these models, the paper develops an efficient Gibbs sampler using uniformization and the forward-backward algorithm. Population genetics motivates the approach, and the authors demonstrate its usefulness for genotype imputation with both phased and unphased SNP data. The work therefore joins a flexible model of changing group structure with an inference procedure and a concrete application to recovering missing genetic information.
neurips-2011-modelling-genetic-variation.tldr: Fragmentation-coagulation processes model sequences through splitting and merging clusters, with efficient inference demonstrated on genotype imputation.

paragraphs: Large collections of unlabeled text can provide word representations for supervised language-processing tasks. This paper targets three shortcomings of existing approaches described by the authors: slow training, failure to model word context, and limited theoretical grounding. Its proposed method, Low Rank Multi-View Learning, learns low-dimensional representations that are specific to a word's context.

LR-MVL uses a fast spectral method to estimate those representations from unlabeled data. The learned representations then serve as features for a supervised learner, allowing representation learning and task-specific training to play separate roles. Context sensitivity matters because the representation incorporates the setting in which a word appears, rather than omitting that information from the feature-learning process.

The authors report very fast training and guaranteed convergence to a global optimum for their method. They also report state-of-the-art performance on named entity recognition and chunking. These findings combine an optimization guarantee with empirical evidence on two language tasks. The contribution is a theoretically grounded, computationally efficient route from unlabeled text to context-specific features usable by supervised classifiers.
neurips-2011-multi-view-learning-of-word.tldr: LR-MVL uses fast spectral learning to produce context-specific word representations with global-optimum convergence and strong results on two NLP tasks.

paragraphs: Variational Message Passing turns Variational Bayes inference into a modular algorithm, but its standard form applies only to conjugate exponential-family models. That mathematical restriction limits which model components can be handled directly. This paper proposes Non-conjugate Variational Message Passing to alleviate the restriction while retaining the organizational benefits of message-based inference.

The extension aims to preserve modularity, allow different ways of calculating expectations, and integrate with the existing Infer.NET framework. These goals matter together: broadening the model family is more useful when individual components can still be combined and inference calculations can be adapted to the components involved. The paper demonstrates the approach on logistic binary regression and multinomial regression.

For multinomial regression, the authors introduce a new variational bound for the softmax factor. It is tighter than other commonly used bounds while remaining computationally tractable. This supplies a more faithful tractable approximation for that part of the model. The work combines a broader message-passing framework with a specific mathematical improvement for handling multinomial outcomes.
neurips-2011-non-conjugate-variational-m.tldr: Non-conjugate Variational Message Passing extends modular Bayesian inference and introduces a tighter tractable softmax bound for multinomial regression.

paragraphs: Learning theory often studies either independent samples from a fixed distribution or sequences chosen by an unrestricted worst-case adversary. This paper develops a framework spanning the space between those extremes. It defines the minimax value of a learning game in which the adversary's available moves are restricted, allowing both stochastic and non-stochastic assumptions about the data.

Using sequential symmetrization, the authors introduce a distribution-dependent form of Rademacher complexity. This quantity provides a way to analyze learning difficulty across the spectrum from independent sampling to worst-case sequences. The resulting bounds also yield variation-type bounds, connecting the restrictions placed on data generation with the performance guarantees available to the learner.

The paper additionally examines smoothed online learning, where noise perturbs the learning setting. It shows that an exponentially small amount of noise can make function classes with infinite Littlestone dimension learnable. This is a possibility established in the studied setting, not a universal claim about every noisy problem. It demonstrates how small changes to adversarial assumptions can substantially alter learnability.
neurips-2011-online-learning-stochastic-.tldr: A framework for restricted adversaries connects stochastic and worst-case online learning and shows that tiny noise can enable learnability.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using side information while learning from uncertain outcomes. This paper derives a data-dependent regret bound for each round in the stochastic setting. Its distinguishing feature is that the bound accounts for how much context the algorithm actually uses to select actions, measured through mutual information between contexts and actions.

For N contexts, the stated scaling involves the square root of N times that mutual information. When the algorithm uses all side information, the bound scales as the square root of N log K, where K is the number of actions. If less information is used, the bound can be substantially tighter. In the zero-mutual-information case, the abstract reports only logarithmic dependence on the number of contexts.

This analysis supports providing abundant side information while charging the algorithm for the information that actually influences its choices. It therefore distinguishes information availability from information use. The paper also presents a contextual-bandit algorithm with computational complexity linear in the number of actions, pairing the theoretical analysis with an algorithmic contribution.
neurips-2011-pac-bayesian-analysis-of-co.tldr: A per-round contextual-bandit regret bound adapts to the mutual information between contexts and chosen actions, penalizing information actually used.

paragraphs: Wide neural networks can have many connections between successive layers, with parameter counts typically growing quadratically in layer width. Local receptive fields control that growth by restricting which lower-level features connect to higher-level units. This paper addresses how to choose those restricted connections when a useful arrangement cannot readily be specified by hand.

The proposed method groups lower-level features according to their pairwise similarity. Features that resemble one another are placed together in receptive fields. The method is fast and can be incorporated into a wide range of unsupervised training procedures, extending the benefits of restricted connectivity to settings without an obvious spatial or topographic arrangement.

The intended benefits include improved scalability and reduced data requirements associated with local receptive fields. The authors show that the approach supports successful multilayer networks even with simple unsupervised training algorithms. They report state-of-the-art accuracies of 82.0% on CIFAR and 60.1% on STL. The results support learning the organization of connections from feature similarity as a practical component of deep feature learning.
neurips-2011-selecting-receptive-fields-.tldr: Selecting receptive fields by feature similarity enables scalable multilayer unsupervised learning without requiring hand-designed connectivity.

paragraphs: A multiclass predictor assigns an object to one of several possible classes. As the number of classes grows, using separate features for each class can make the predictor increasingly expensive. This paper studies predictors that use a small pool of features shared across classes, with the goal that feature count grows more slowly than class count.

The authors introduce ShareBoost and analyze its ability to find such predictors. Their guarantee is conditional: if a predictor using few shared features exists, ShareBoost efficiently finds a predictor with that property and small generalization error. This links economical feature use with performance on unseen examples, rather than treating a small feature set as the only objective.

The paper also explains how ShareBoost can learn a nonlinear predictor with fast evaluation. That extends the computational motivation beyond the feature count alone to the cost of making predictions. Experiments on natural datasets demonstrate benefits and compare the method with state-of-the-art approaches. The central contribution is an algorithmic and theoretical route to sharing useful features across many classification decisions.
neurips-2011-shareboost-efficient-multic.tldr: ShareBoost efficiently learns multiclass predictors using few shared features when such predictors exist, with generalization guarantees and fast nonlinear evaluation.

paragraphs: A similarity or distance function can describe how examples relate without directly specifying a classifier. This paper asks what makes such a function useful for a particular classification task. It introduces a framework for defining that usefulness and algorithms with generalization guarantees when the similarity function satisfies the resulting criterion.

The framework allows the data to determine the appropriate notion of usefulness instead of imposing one fixed criterion across tasks. The authors provide theoretical guarantees that a suitable criterion can itself be learned. Their formulation also unifies and extends earlier frameworks, connecting the choice of similarity-based representation with the requirements of the learning problem.

To construct a classifier, the method uses landmark points as references for representing examples. The paper adds a diversity-based heuristic that selects landmarks for the task rather than choosing them randomly. Experiments on similarity-learning datasets and UCI benchmarks support both criterion learning and landmark selection, with consistently significant improvements over the evaluated approaches. The theoretical guarantees and empirical landmark results provide complementary support for adapting the representation to the data.
neurips-2011-similarity-based-learning-v.tldr: Learning task-specific similarity criteria and selecting diverse landmarks produces data-adapted classifiers with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: This paper considers optimization when the learner can query a point and receive only a noisy observation of the function's value there. The objective is convex and Lipschitz, and the allowed query points form a compact convex set. These assumptions describe the optimization problem studied; the feedback does not directly provide the function's gradient or its values elsewhere.

The authors develop a generalization of the ellipsoid algorithm for this stochastic bandit-feedback setting. They analyze cumulative regret, which captures the cost of the points selected while searching for a good solution. The resulting upper bound grows with the square root of the number of rounds T, multiplied by a factor polynomial in the dimension d.

A corresponding lower bound shows that any algorithm must incur regret of at least square-root order in T on this problem. The proposed method therefore achieves optimal scaling with the time horizon. That optimality statement specifically concerns dependence on T: the reported upper bound also includes a polynomial dependence on dimension. The result establishes the achievable time scaling despite noisy, value-only feedback.
neurips-2011-stochastic-convex-optimizat.tldr: A generalized ellipsoid algorithm achieves optimal square-root dependence on time for stochastic convex optimization with noisy value-only feedback.

paragraphs: Loopy belief propagation is widely used for inference in graphical models, but its empirical success exceeds the available theoretical guarantees. Strong interactions between variables make its behavior especially difficult to analyze because of underlying phase transitions. This paper focuses on whether the algorithm has a unique fixed point, a state that remains unchanged by its updates.

The authors derive a necessary-and-sufficient condition expressed through graph structure and interaction signs. Each sign identifies an interaction as attractive or repulsive. This shifts attention toward the arrangement and types of relationships in the graph. Earlier uniqueness guarantees, as characterized in the abstract, required interaction strengths to be sufficiently small in particular senses.

For the specified class of signed graphs, the new condition covers arbitrarily strong interactions. That scope is essential: the result does not assert uniqueness for every graph with strong interactions. The proof builds on a connection between belief propagation and the graph zeta function. Its significance is a structural characterization of fixed-point uniqueness that extends beyond weak-interaction guarantees within the covered graph class.
neurips-2011-uniqueness-of-belief-propag.tldr: A graph-and-sign condition characterizes belief-propagation fixed-point uniqueness and covers arbitrarily strong interactions within a specified signed-graph class.
